report:
## Conclusion: The claim is **false** — there is no scientific evidence that drinking boiled garlic water cures COVID-19.

This myth circulated widely on social media early in the pandemic (beginning around February 2020), but health authorities and fact-checkers have consistently debunked it.

### Key findings:

1. **The World Health Organization (WHO)** explicitly addresses garlic in its COVID-19 "Mythbusters" section, confirming there is no evidence that eating garlic (or drinking garlic water) protects against or cures COVID-19. WHO's Dr. Sylvie Briand also addressed this myth directly in a "Science in 5" podcast episode. ([https://www.who.int/emergencies/diseases/novel-coronavirus-2019/advice-for-public/myth-busters](https://www.who.int/emergencies/diseases/novel-coronavirus-2019/advice-for-public/myth-busters); [https://www.who.int/podcasts/series/science-in-5/episode--8---myth-vs-science](https://www.who.int/podcasts/series/science-in-5/episode--8---myth-vs-science))

2. **FactCheck.org** published a detailed article in February 2020 concluding that garlic is not a cure for COVID-19, noting that while garlic has some known health properties, no evidence supports its use against the novel coronavirus. ([https://www.factcheck.org/2020/02/fake-coronavirus-cures-part-2-garlic-isnt-a-cure/](https://www.factcheck.org/2020/02/fake-coronavirus-cures-part-2-garlic-isnt-a-cure/))

3. **AFP Fact Check** also investigated a related claim (a tonic of onions, ginger, garlic, and lemon) and found no scientific proof it can cure COVID-19, with health professionals confirming the lack of evidence. ([https://factcheck.afp.com/theres-no-scientific-proof-tonic-onions-ginger-garlic-and-lemon-can-cure-covid-19](https://factcheck.afp.com/theres-no-scientific-proof-tonic-onions-ginger-garlic-and-lemon-can-cure-covid-19))

4. **A peer-reviewed review** in the *Journal of Clinical Medicine* acknowledges garlic's general antiviral properties (due to organosulfur compounds like allicin) but does not claim it prevents or cures COVID-19 specifically. Having general antiviral properties in laboratory settings is very different from being a proven treatment for a specific disease. ([https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC7434784/](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC7434784/))

### Bottom line:
Garlic does have some general antimicrobial and antioxidant properties, but no clinical evidence supports drinking boiled garlic water as a cure or treatment for COVID-19. Relying on this remedy could be dangerous if it delays seeking proper medical care.
